The number of CUDA cores on the GPU
Whether a CUDA-capable GPU and compatible driver are visible to this PyTorch build
The current GPU utilization percentage
questions.explain: `torch.cuda.is_available()` is a boolean check for whether PyTorch can see a usable CUDA GPU and driver — used to pick a device gracefully.

questions.q: Why must `inputs = inputs.to(device)` reassign the variable, while `model = model.to(device)` technically doesn't need to?
options: A tensor's `.to()` returns a new tensor (the original is unchanged), while a module's `.to()` moves its parameters in place
There is no actual difference; both are purely stylistic
Reassignment is required only when using `.cuda()`
`.to()` only works on models, not tensors
questions.explain: Calling `.to()` on a tensor produces a new tensor object, leaving the original untouched, so the result must be captured. A module's `.to()` mutates its parameters and buffers in place.

options: `.cuda()` is deprecated and no longer works in PyTorch
`.to(device)` uses the same code path regardless of whether the target is CPU, CUDA, or another backend, avoiding hardcoded device branches
`.to(device)` is faster at the hardware level
`.cuda()` only works with integer tensors
questions.explain: `.to(device)` lets the same code run correctly whatever `device` resolves to, while `.cuda()` hardcodes a CUDA GPU specifically.

questions.q: A RuntimeError says 'Expected all tensors to be on the same device, but found at least two devices, cuda:0 and cpu'. What is the most likely cause?
options: The GPU has run out of memory
CUDA is not installed on the system
The model has too many layers
A tensor — often created fresh with something like `torch.zeros(...)` without a `device=` argument — defaulted to CPU and was never moved to the GPU
questions.explain: This error almost always traces back to one tensor that was created on the default device (CPU) and never explicitly moved, meeting a GPU tensor in an operation.

questions.q: What is the advantage of writing `device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")` instead of hardcoding `"cuda"`?
options: It automatically enables mixed precision
The same script can run on a machine without a GPU, falling back to CPU instead of crashing
It reduces GPU memory usage
It runs faster on a GPU
questions.explain: Checking availability once and storing the result means the script degrades gracefully to CPU execution rather than raising an error on a machine with no GPU.
